Love Beads
LUV BEEDZ
noun (Boomer slang)
Love + beads (Old English gebed, a prayer — from the counting of prayers on a string, whence bead for any small pierced ball). Love beads, strings of colorful glass or wooden beads worn by hippies of both sexes as a token of peace and love, often handmade and exchanged as gifts, were a fashion of 1967–70; they drew partly on Eastern prayer beads (the Hindu and Buddhist mala) that came into the counterculture with Hare Krishna and Transcendental Meditation.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Love beads were the hippie’s necklace: strands of bright beads worn by young men and women alike as a badge of peace and love, sometimes exchanged as gifts, sometimes borrowed from Eastern prayer practice. The Christian observation: the word bead itself once meant a prayer — the old English gebed — because beads were used to count prayers. Love beads took the form and emptied it, or filled it with Eastern mysticism. Scripture has a great deal to say about ornaments around the neck, and it points them toward wisdom and truth. "For they shall be an ornament of grace unto thy head, and chains about thy neck" (Pro 1:9) — said of a father’s instruction and a mother’s law. "Let not mercy and truth forsake thee: bind them about thy neck; write them upon the table of thine heart" (Pro 3:3). Scripture also knows how ornaments can go wrong. Isaiah’s daughters of Zion wore "tinkling ornaments ... The chains, and the bracelets" (Isa 3:18–19) to display their pride, and Aaron melted down Israel’s earrings to make the golden calf (Exo 32:2). And Peter tells believers not to make outward adorning their glory but "the hidden man of the heart" (1Pe 3:4). A string of beads is no sin. But the best love beads a child can wear are the ones Proverbs describes: a father’s wisdom and a mother’s law, mercy and truth, bound about the neck and written on the heart.

Webster 1828 Definition

Hippie necklaces (1967–70) of colorful beads worn as tokens of peace and love, partly borrowed from Eastern prayer beads — Scripture’s better necklace is mercy and truth bound about the neck (Pro 3:3) and a parent’s instruction as chains of grace (Pro 1:9).

LOVE BEADS, n. pl. (Boomer slang, 1967–70) Strings of colorful beads worn, especially by hippies, as a symbol of peace and love; often handmade and given as gifts.

Webster (1828) — BEAD, noun 1. A little perforated ball, to be strung on a thread, and worn about the neck, for ornament. A string of beads is called a necklace. Beads are made of gold, pearl, amber, steel, garnet, coral, diamond, crystal, pastes, glasses, etc. The Romanists use strings of beads in rehearsing their prayers. Hence the phrase, to tell beads, and to be at one’s beads, is to be at prayer. 2. Any small globular body; hence the glass globules, used in traffic with savages, and sold in strings, are called beads; also a bubble on spirit. 3. In architecture, a round molding, commonly made upon the edge of a piece of stuff, in the Corinthian and Roman orders, cut or carved in short embossments, like beads in necklaces.of beads, is a charge given by a priest to his parishioners, to repeat certain pater-nosters upon their beads for a departed soul.

Decode for families: bead once meant "prayer." Ask what your child’s bracelets are for.

Isa 3:19 — "The chains, and the bracelets, and the mufflers,"

Modern Corruption

Love beads borrowed the form of prayer beads and filled it with sentiment or Eastern mysticism; Scripture binds mercy and truth about the neck and warns of ornaments that serve pride or idols.

expand to see more

The love bead was a gentle fashion with a religious shadow. Many hippies wore beads borrowed from Hindu and Buddhist practice, and the counterculture’s turn east — Hare Krishna, Transcendental Meditation, the Beatles in India in 1968 — brought prayer beads into American wardrobes stripped of their meaning or loaded with another. Every generation has its version; today it may be crystal bracelets for "energy" or charm bracelets for luck. The Christian asks of any ornament: what is it for?

Proverbs answers with a beautiful image. The best necklace a young person can wear is the instruction of godly parents (Pro 1:9), and mercy and truth bound about the neck (Pro 3:3). Those beads do not break or fade, and they are visible in every conversation.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old English gebed (a prayer) → Middle English bede (a prayer; a prayer-bead) → bead (any small pierced ball) + love → 1967–70 love beads.

expand to see more

Old English gebed — a prayer; biddan — to pray, to ask

Middle English bede — a prayer; the small balls on which prayers were counted

English bead — any small perforated ball strung for ornament (1828)

1967–70: love beads — hippie necklaces; Eastern mala influence

Hebrew anaq — to put on as a necklace; chains about the neck (Pro 1:9)
